A '''capsule''' ({{etymology|la|{{wikt-lang|la|capsula}}|small box or chest}}), or '''[[stadium (geometry)|stadium]] of revolution''', is a basic [[three-dimensional space|three-dimensional]] [[geometric shape]] consisting of a [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinder]] with [[Sphere#Hemisphere|hemispherical]] ends.<ref>{{cite journal

 | volume = 56
 | year = 1997
 | bibcode = 1997PhRvE..56.1102S
 }}</ref> Another name for this shape is '''spherocylinder'''.<ref name="K1951">{{cite journal

}}</ref><ref name="F1987"/><ref name="DSL2000">{{cite journal

It can also be referred to as an [[oval]] although the sides (either vertical or horizontal) are straight [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]].

== Usages ==
The shape is used for some objects like [[Pressure vessel#Cylindrical vessel with hemispherical ends|containers for pressurised gases]], [[Dome|building domes]], and [[capsule (pharmacy)|pharmaceutical capsules]].

In [[chemistry]] and [[physics]], this shape is used as a basic model for non-spherical particles. It appears, in particular as a model for the molecules in [[liquid crystal]]s<ref>{{cite journal
| last=Onsager | first=Lars | authorlink=Lars Onsager
| title=The effects of shape on the interaction of colloidal particles
| journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
| volume=51
| issue=4
| date=May 1949
| pages=627–659
| doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1949.tb27296.x| bibcode=1949NYASA..51..627O | s2cid=84562683 }}</ref><ref name="F1987">{{cite journal
| first=Daan | last=Frenkel
| title=Onsager's spherocylinders revisited
| journal=Journal of Physical Chemistry
| date=September 10, 1987
| volume=91
| issue=19
| pages=4912–4916
| doi=10.1021/j100303a008| bibcode=1987JPhCh..91.4912F
| hdl=1874/8823
| s2cid=96013495
| hdl-access=free
}}</ref><ref name="DSL2000"/> or for the particles in [[Granular material|granular matter]].<ref name="PWTFRL2005" /><ref name="PL2005"/><ref name="PL2009"/>

==Formulas==
The volume <math>V</math> of a capsule is calculated by adding the volume of a ball of radius <math>r</math> (that accounts for the two hemispheres) to the volume of the cylindrical part. Hence, if the cylinder has height <math>h</math>,

:<math>V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 + (\pi r^2h)= \pi r^2 \left (\frac{4}{3}r + h \right )</math>.
 
The surface area of a capsule of radius <math>r</math> whose cylinder part has height <math>h</math> is <math>2 \pi r (2r + h)</math>.

==Generalization==

A capsule can be equivalently described as the [[Minkowski sum]] of a ball of radius <math>r</math> with a [[line segment]] of length <math>a</math>.<ref name="PWTFRL2005"/> By this description, capsules can be straightforwardly generalized as Minkowski sums of a ball with a [[polyhedron]]. The resulting shape is called a spheropolyhedron.<ref name="PL2005">{{cite conference

| pages=1375–1378
| url=https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/77616}}</ref><ref name="PL2009">{{cite book

==Related shapes==

A capsule is the three-dimensional shape obtained by revolving the two-dimensional [[Stadium (geometry)|stadium]] around the [[line of symmetry]] that [[bisection|bisects]] the [[semicircle|semicircles]].
